title: YOU’RE PROBABLY A GOOD PERSON. ROMANS 3:23 SAYS THAT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH.
paragraphs: YOU’RE PROBABLY A GOOD PERSON. ROMANS 3:23 SAYS THAT STILL ISN’T ENOUGH.
What “All Have Sinned and Fall Short” Really Says About Human Goodness—and Why the Verse That Humiliates Our Pride May Be One of the Most Hope-Filled Sentences Ever Written
There is a sentence almost nobody wants to hear.
Especially the person who has tried to live decently.
You worked for what you have.
You love your children.
You help people when you can.

You have never murdered anyone. You are not robbing houses. You are not deliberately destroying lives. Maybe you give to people who need help. Maybe you have stayed beside someone in a hospital room. Maybe you have forgiven things nobody knows you had to forgive.
And when you look at some of the darkness in this world, there is a thought that can quietly rise inside you:
I know I’m not perfect… but surely I’m a good person.
Then Romans 3 walks into the room.
And it refuses to flatter you.
But if you stay long enough, you discover something astonishing.
It refuses to flatter you because God intends to give you something infinitely better than flattery.
Grace.
Paul writes:
Pantes gar hēmarton kai hysterountai tēs doxēs tou theou.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The sentence is short.
Its implications are devastating.
And its next words are breathtaking.
Because Romans 3:23 was never meant to be ripped away from Romans 3:24.
Paul continues:
“δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτοῦ χάριτι…”
Being justified freely—without payment, without earning it—by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That changes everything.
The scandal is not merely that sinners are worse than they think.
The greater scandal is that God’s grace is better than sinners could ever deserve.
Maybe you have heard Romans 3:23 used like a hammer.
“All have sinned.”
End of discussion.
But Paul was not writing a slogan. He was constructing an argument that systematically dismantles every human hiding place so that every sinner can see why Jesus Christ is not merely helpful.
He is necessary.
And that includes the respectable sinner.
The generous sinner.
The religious sinner.
The churchgoing sinner.
The sinner who volunteers.
The sinner who pays his bills.
The sinner everybody calls “a wonderful person.”
And yes…
the sinner writing these words.
The sinner reading them.
“All.”
The Greek begins with πάντες—pantes.
All.
Not merely notorious people.
Not merely criminals.
Not merely adulterers, addicts, abusers, hypocrites, liars, thieves, or people whose scandals became public.
All.
That word leaves no VIP entrance into the kingdom of God.
No résumé.
No family name.
No denomination.
No charitable record.
No amount of religious activity.
No secret folder marked, “But look at all the good things I did.”
And here is where Romans 3 is sometimes misunderstood.
Paul is not saying human beings are incapable of doing anything that appears genuinely kind or beneficial toward another person.
A non-Christian can feed someone who is hungry.
An unbelieving father can sacrifice for his children.
An atheist can return a lost wallet.
A person who does not know Christ can give money to the poor, care for a dying parent, rescue someone in danger, show patience to a child, or perform extraordinary acts of civic courage.
Christians do not need to deny obvious human kindness in order to defend biblical truth.
The question Romans 3 forces upon us is deeper.
Not:
Have you ever done something good?
But:
Are you righteous before a perfectly holy God?
Those are radically different questions.
Imagine standing beside an ocean holding a glass of clean water.
The water may really be clean.
But nobody would confuse your glass with the ocean.

In a similar way, human beings can perform acts that are good in a real, creaturely, social sense while still falling infinitely short of God's perfect holiness and having no goodness capable of cancelling our guilt.
Our mistake is comparing horizontally.
We look sideways.
We compare ourselves with the alcoholic.
The adulterer.
The corrupt politician.
The abusive father.
The woman who abandoned her children.
The man in prison.
The hypocrite exposed on television.
And suddenly we feel clean.
But Romans 3 turns our face upward.
The standard is not your neighbor.
The standard is not the worst person you know.
The standard is not whether society considers you respectable.
Paul says humanity falls short of the glory of God.
That is an entirely different measurement.
You can be taller than every person standing beside you and still be nowhere near touching the stars.
And that is why comparison is such a dangerous spiritual anesthetic.
It can make a dying person feel healthy simply because somebody nearby appears sicker.
You say:
“I have never cheated on my spouse.”
Good.
But have you loved God perfectly?
“I give to charity.”
Good.
But has every motive of your heart always been pure?
“I never killed anyone.”
Good.
But have hatred, bitterness, contempt, revenge, or cruelty ever found shelter inside you?
“I go to church.”
Good.
But have you ever worshiped while your heart was miles away?
“I help people.”
Good.
But have you never secretly wanted recognition for being the person who helps?
“I believe in God.”
Even then the question remains:
Have you loved Him with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength every moment of your life?
Suddenly the courtroom becomes quiet.
Because the Gospel does not merely examine the polished exterior.
God sees the heart.
He sees the generosity that secretly wanted applause.
The apology designed to end an argument rather than heal a wound.
The prayer spoken publicly while resentment remained privately protected.
The worship song sung while pride sat comfortably on the throne.
The kindness performed partly because we wanted to believe something good about ourselves.
And even our genuinely loving acts cannot travel backward through history and erase sins already committed.
You cannot hug enough people today to make yesterday’s lie become truth.
You cannot donate enough money tomorrow to make yesterday’s lust become purity.
You cannot serve enough meals to make yesterday’s hatred become love.
Good works are good.
But good works are terrible saviors.
They were never designed to carry the weight of your eternity.
This is where the Gospel becomes offensive to human pride.
We desperately want to contribute something to the verdict.
Surely God will place our sins on one side of a scale and our kindness on the other.
Surely He will notice that we tried.
Surely heaven contains some divine accounting department where our good deeds can compensate for our rebellion.
But Scripture destroys that fantasy.

Paul says salvation is by grace through faith, not from ourselves, not from works so that nobody can boast. And then—beautifully—he says those who belong to Christ are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
Not good works therefore Christ accepts us.
Christ saves us therefore a transformed life begins producing good works.
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are fruit growing from a life touched by grace.
The Gospel does not say:
“Become good enough and Jesus will take you.”
It says:
“You cannot make yourself righteous before God, so Jesus came for sinners.”
That is why Christ matters.
If human goodness could save us, Calvary becomes unnecessary.
If moral improvement could reconcile us to God, Jesus could have remained in heaven and sent us better instructions.
If salvation were simply “try harder,” humanity needed a coach.
If salvation were simply education, humanity needed a teacher.
If salvation were simply inspiration, humanity needed a motivational speaker.
But Scripture says we needed redemption.
We needed a Savior.
We needed Jesus.
The cross announces something simultaneously humiliating and glorious:
Your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
God's grace was great enough that Christ willingly did.
And perhaps that is what hurts.
Because grace does something human pride hates.
Grace removes bragging rights.
At the foot of the cross, the respectable businessman kneels beside the recovering addict.
The pastor kneels beside the prisoner.
The lifelong church member kneels beside the prodigal who wasted twenty years.
The virgin kneels beside the former prostitute.
The person whose sins were hidden kneels beside the person whose sins became headlines.
Nobody arrives holding a trophy.
Nobody walks through heaven saying, “I knew I was better than them.”
We come empty-handed.
We come guilty.
We come needing mercy.
And somehow this is not bad news.
It is liberation.
Because if salvation depended upon you becoming good enough, when would you finally know that you had done enough?
How many prayers?
How many donations?
How many years of obedience?
How many tears?
How many Bible chapters?
How many people helped?
How many temptations resisted?
How much regret would finally pay the debt?
You would spend your entire life staring at yourself.
Was I sincere enough?
Did I repent enough?
Did I serve enough?
Did I sacrifice enough?
Am I finally enough?
The Gospel turns your eyes away from your résumé and toward a cross.
Toward Christ.
Toward blood shed for sinners.
Toward a Savior who does what human morality never could.
And maybe this is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs:
You do not need to pretend you are better than you are when your hope rests in Someone infinitely better than you could ever be.
That is freedom.
You can finally confess.
You can finally stop hiding.
You can finally say:
“Yes. I sinned.”
“Yes. I hurt people.”
“Yes. There are things I regret.”
“Yes. Some of my motives were ugly.”
“Yes. I knew better.”
“Yes. I walked away.”
“Yes. I looked religious while hiding things.”
“Yes. I need mercy.”
Because Christianity does not begin when a bad person successfully convinces God that he is good.
Christianity begins when a sinner stops defending himself and runs to Christ.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
It is surrendering our excuses.
It is agreeing with God about sin and turning toward the Savior.
And there is another side we cannot miss.
Once grace finds you, grace does not give you permission to remain comfortably unchanged.
The Christ who forgives also transforms.
The Gospel is not:
“You sinned, but don't worry about it.”
It is:
“You sinned. Christ died and rose. Come to Him. Receive mercy. Follow Him. Let Him remake what sin distorted.”
Jesus does not merely improve the public relations surrounding your scandal.
He begins rewriting the person.
Pride begins learning humility.
Greed begins learning generosity.
Lust begins learning purity.
Bitterness begins learning forgiveness.
Selfishness begins learning sacrifice.
A liar begins learning truth.
A taker begins becoming a giver.
A person who once lived entirely for himself begins whispering something that would once have sounded impossible:
“Jesus, my life belongs to You.”
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
Not without battles.
But genuinely.
That is why Christian good works matter enormously.
Not because they purchase heaven.
Because they reveal the transforming fingerprints of the One who saved us.
You are not saved because you performed enough good works.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ—and the grace that saves begins teaching your life a different way to walk.
That means Romans 3:23 is not permission to shrug and say, “Everybody sins, so who cares?”
Quite the opposite.
Everybody sins.
Therefore everybody desperately needs Jesus.
Including your father.
Your daughter.
Your closest friend.
Your coworker.
Your spouse.
The person you cannot stand.
The person everyone admires.
The person secretly falling apart tonight.
And the person staring back at you from the mirror.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe there was never a viral post.
No police report.
No affair exposed.
No addiction discovered.
No dramatic testimony.
Maybe your scandal lived entirely behind your ribs.
Pride.
Envy.
Secret lust.
Coldness toward God.
Resentment.
Self-righteousness.
Years spent believing you were good because you had carefully chosen worse people as your measuring stick.
God saw it.
And still the Gospel came looking for you.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your sin never mattered.
God dealing with sin through Jesus Christ.
Not God lowering holiness until you could reach it.
Christ coming down to rescue those who could not climb high enough.
Not good people earning their way into God's family.
Sinners receiving what they could never purchase.
That is the scandal of grace.
And perhaps the greatest shock of Romans 3:23 is that verse 23 does not get the final word.
Verse 24 follows it.
Sin does not get the final word.
Grace speaks.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Christ speaks.
Your worst chapter does not automatically become the ending.
Jesus still writes.
So stop presenting God with your moral résumé.
Bring Him your surrender.
Stop saying, “At least I'm better than…”
Look at Jesus.
Stop asking whether you have accumulated enough goodness to deserve Him.
You haven't.
Neither have I.
That is precisely why grace is grace.
Come empty-handed.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come trusting not in your record, but in Christ.
Talk to Jesus.
Right there.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Confess what He already knows.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust in Christ.
Someone reading the same comments may realize tonight that they are not the only person still fighting.
Your honesty may become another person's courage.
And please don't keep this article inside a private religious bubble.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” somehow proves your Christianity. It cannot.
It isn't.
Somebody may need to discover that Jesus did not come merely to make good people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
There will probably come a day when pride tells you, “You're doing pretty well.”
Or shame tells you, “You've done too much.”
Come back and remember:
Neither pride nor shame gets to define the Gospel.
Jesus does.
And there is much more waiting for believers who are serious about growing.
But remember what matters most.
Sharing this article cannot save you.
Owning Christian books cannot save you.
Being generous cannot save you.
Being religious cannot save you.
Being nicer than the person next door cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And once that truth reaches the deepest place in your heart, Romans 3:23 stops sounding merely like an accusation.
It becomes the doorway to astonishing hope.
“All have sinned.”
Yes.
You too.
Me too.
Every one of us.
But the sentence continues into grace.
The guilty can be justified.
The ashamed can come into the light.
The proud can finally put down their trophies.
The broken can stop pretending.
The sinner can come home.
Not because human goodness finally became impressive enough for God…
but because Jesus Christ was always enough for sinners.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
When your goodness runs out and your excuses finally fall silent, you may discover that Jesus was never waiting for your résumé—He was calling for your surrender.
